title: Unit 2: Parallel Lines & Triangles
text:
When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, it creates 8 angles with predictable relationships:

Corresponding angles (same position at each intersection): congruent
Alternate interior angles (between the two lines, opposite sides of the transversal): congruent
Alternate exterior angles (outside the two lines, opposite sides): congruent
Co-interior / same-side interior angles (between the lines, same side): supplementary







TipThe shortcut



If the lines are parallel: angles in matching positions are congruent, “alternate” pairs are congruent, and any pair that’s between the lines and on the same side adds to 180°.






Triangle Angle Sum Theorem: the three interior angles of any triangle always add to 180°.
Exterior Angle Theorem: an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote (non-adjacent) interior angles.
Isosceles Triangle Theorem: if two sides of a triangle are congruent, the angles opposite those sides are congruent (and vice versa).

title: Unit 2: Parallel Lines & Triangles
text:
Practice Problems

Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle measures 65°. Find the measure of its co-interior (same-side interior) angle.







NoteSolution





Co-interior angles are supplementary: 180° − 65° = 115°




A triangle has angles measuring 40° and 75°. Find the third angle, then find the exterior angle adjacent to it.







NoteSolution





Third interior angle: 180° − 40° − 75° = 65° The exterior angle adjacent to it is supplementary to it: 180° − 65° = 115°
(Check with the Exterior Angle Theorem: 40° + 75° = 115°. ✓ It matches, since the exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.)




An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°. Find the two base angles.







NoteSolution





The two base angles are congruent to each other, and all three angles sum to 180°: 180° − 40° = 140°, split evenly: 140° ÷ 2 = 70° each

title: Geometry
text:
Advanced geometry builds on algebra by introducing formal logical reasoning — you’re not just solving for x anymore, you’re proving why something must be true. These units move from vocabulary and postulates to triangle relationships and proof-writing.

Units

Foundations & Proof Basics — points/lines/planes, angle pairs, intro to two-column proofs
Parallel Lines & Triangles — parallel line angle relationships, triangle angle theorems
Congruence & Similarity — congruence shortcuts (SSS, SAS…), similarity, right triangle basics







Note



Later units (quadrilaterals, circles, area/volume, trigonometry) can follow this same page structure.






 Back to top

title: Unit 2: Rhetoric & Argumentative Writing
text:
Ethos: appeals to credibility/character (“As a doctor with 20 years of experience…”)
Pathos: appeals to emotion (vivid stories, emotionally charged language)
Logos: appeals to logic (statistics, reasoning, cause-and-effect)

Strong arguments usually blend all three rather than relying on just one.



Before analyzing or writing an argument, identify:

Author — who is speaking, and what’s their credibility/bias?
Audience — who is this trying to persuade, and what do they already believe?
Purpose — what does the author want the audience to think or do?
Context — what’s happening around this text that shapes it?





Thesis: a clear, arguable claim (not a fact, not a question) — should be specific enough that someone could reasonably disagree.
Body paragraphs: each should have one main point (topic sentence), evidence, and analysis that ties back to the thesis.
Counterargument: acknowledge the strongest opposing view, then rebut it — this makes your argument look stronger, not weaker.
Conclusion: don’t just restate the thesis — address the “so what?” (why does this argument matter?).







TipTesting a thesis



Ask: “could a reasonable person disagree with this?” If not, it’s a fact, not an arguable thesis. “Recycling reduces landfill waste” is a fact. “Mandatory recycling programs are more effective than voluntary ones” is arguable.

title: Unit 2: Rhetoric & Argumentative Writing
text:
Practice Problems

Identify the appeal: “Over 10,000 peer-reviewed studies confirm this treatment’s effectiveness.”







NoteSolution





Logos — it uses statistics/data as logical evidence.




Rewrite this weak thesis into an arguable one: “Social media has both good and bad effects on teenagers.”







NoteSolution





Sample fix: “While social media offers useful ways for teenagers to connect, its design features (infinite scroll, algorithmic feeds) create outsized harm to teen mental health that outweighs its benefits.” (Key fix: pick a side and make a specific, debatable claim instead of listing both sides neutrally.)




Why should you include a counterargument in your own essay instead of only presenting your own side?







NoteSolution





Addressing the strongest opposing view — and then rebutting it — shows you’ve considered the issue fully, which makes your own argument more credible and harder to dismiss. Ignoring counterarguments can make your essay look one-sided or unaware of obvious objections.

title: Language Arts
text:
High school language arts asks you to do three things at a higher level than before: read texts closely and explain how they create meaning, build persuasive arguments, and write with precise, correct mechanics.

Grammar & Mechanics — clauses, common errors, and punctuation rules that trip people up







Note



Later units (research writing, vocabulary/etymology, specific texts) can follow this same page structure.

title: Unit 3: Culture
text:
Culture is a group’s shared beliefs, practices, technology, and values, passed down and modified over time. The cultural landscape is the visible imprint of culture on the land (buildings, farms, road layouts, signage).

Cultural traits: individual elements of culture (a specific food, style of dress, custom)
Cultural complex: a related set of traits (traits around a specific religion, for example)
Cultural region: an area sharing common cultural traits/complexes





Relocation diffusion: culture spreads because people physically move (immigrants bringing food traditions).
Expansion diffusion: culture spreads outward from its origin while staying strong there, split into:

Contagious diffusion: spreads quickly through direct contact, most people affected (a viral trend)
Hierarchical diffusion: spreads through a ranked order — big cities first, then smaller towns (new fashion trends, tech adoption)
Stimulus diffusion: the underlying idea spreads even though the specific practice changes (fast food concept adapted with local menus abroad)






Language families (e.g., Indo-European) share a common ancestral root; a lingua franca is a common language used for trade/communication between groups who don’t share a native language (English, historically).
Universalizing religions (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism) actively seek converts and can spread anywhere.
Ethnic religions (Hinduism, Judaism) are closely tied to a specific ethnic group or place and spread mainly by relocation diffusion, not conversion.







TipTelling diffusion types apart



Ask: did it spread because people moved (relocation) or because it spread outward while staying put at the source (expansion)? If expansion, ask if it moved through everyone nearby (contagious), big places to small (hierarchical), or if only the idea survived the trip while the details changed (stimulus).

title: Unit 3: Culture
text:
Practice Problems

A new slang term appears first in a major city and later shows up in smaller towns nearby, following the ranking of city size. What type of diffusion is this?







NoteSolution





Hierarchical diffusion — it spread from larger places down to smaller ones in order of size/importance.




Classify: Buddhism spreading from Asia to the West as immigrants moved and brought their practice with them.







NoteSolution





Relocation diffusion — the religion spread because its practitioners physically relocated.




A burger chain from the US opens overseas but swaps the menu for local flavors and ingredients. What type of diffusion best describes this, and why?







NoteSolution





Stimulus diffusion — the general concept (fast, casual chain food) spread, but the specific product was modified to fit the new cultural context.

title: Unit 2: Population & Migration
text:
Arithmetic density: total population ÷ total land area — simple but can be misleading.
Physiologic density: population ÷ arable (farmable) land — better reflects pressure on food-producing land.
Agricultural density: number of farmers ÷ arable land — reflects efficiency of farming.




A model of how birth rates and death rates change as a country develops, in 5 stages:

Stage 1 (pre-industrial): high birth rate, high death rate → slow growth
Stage 2 (early industrial): death rate drops fast (better medicine/food), birth rate stays high → rapid growth
Stage 3 (industrializing): birth rate starts falling (urbanization, education, women in workforce) → growth slows
Stage 4 (developed): low birth rate, low death rate → slow/stable growth
Stage 5 (some developed nations): birth rate falls below death rate → population decline

Related: the Epidemiologic Transition Model tracks causes of death shifting from infectious disease (Stage 1-2) to chronic/degenerative disease (Stage 4-5).




Push factors: reasons people leave a place (war, famine, lack of jobs)
Pull factors: reasons people are drawn to a place (jobs, safety, family)
Types: forced vs. voluntary; internal (within a country) vs. international
Ravenstein’s Laws of Migration (key ideas): most migrants move only a short distance; long-distance migrants tend to move toward large cities; migration increases as industrialization/transportation improves.







TipCommon mix-up



Physiologic density and arithmetic density use the same numerator (population) but different denominators. A country can look “empty” by arithmetic density (lots of desert/land) yet be very crowded by physiologic density (little arable land) — Egypt is the classic example.

title: Unit 2: Population & Migration
text:
Practice Problems

A country has 40 million people, 1 million km² of total land, and 200,000 km² of arable land. Find its arithmetic and physiologic densities.







NoteSolution





Arithmetic density = 40,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 40 people/km² Physiologic density = 40,000,000 ÷ 200,000 = 200 people/km²
The physiologic density is much higher, showing real pressure on the usable farmland even though the arithmetic density looks moderate.




A country has a high birth rate and a rapidly falling death rate, driven by new medical technology, but women are not yet entering the workforce in large numbers. What DTM stage is this, and what happens to population?







NoteSolution





Stage 2. With births staying high but deaths falling, the natural increase rate spikes — this is the period of the fastest population growth.




Give one push factor and one pull factor for a family relocating from a rural area to a big city for work.







NoteSolution





Push factor: lack of jobs/limited economic opportunity in the rural area. Pull factor: availability of jobs and higher wages in the city. (Any reasonable equivalent, e.g. push = poor schools, pull = better schools, is also correct.)

text:
Hi! This site is our home base for getting ready for high school. Each subject has its own section in the menu above, broken into units. Every unit page has three parts:

title: Chemistry
text:
Chemistry is the study of matter — what it’s made of and how it changes. These units build up from the basics (matter and measurement) to the atomic-level ideas (atomic structure, bonding) you’ll need for everything else in the course.

Units

Matter & Measurement — classifying matter, SI units, significant figures, density
Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — protons/neutrons/electrons, isotopes, periodic trends
Chemical Bonding — ionic vs. covalent bonds, Lewis structures, naming compounds







Note



More units (stoichiometry, reactions, gases, acids & bases) can be added the same way as you move further into the course — just copy the pattern of an existing unit page.






 Back to top

title: Unit 1: Matter & Measurement
text:
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. We classify it like this:

Pure substances — fixed composition

Elements: can’t be broken down further (e.g., oxygen, gold)
Compounds: two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio (e.g., H₂O)

Mixtures — variable composition, physically combined

Homogeneous (uniform throughout, e.g., saltwater)
Heterogeneous (visibly different parts, e.g., salad)


Physical vs. chemical changes: a physical change alters appearance but not identity (melting ice); a chemical change produces a new substance (rusting iron).



Chemists use SI units: mass (kg or g), volume (L or mL), temperature (K), length (m).
Density = mass ÷ volume, usually in g/mL or g/cm³. It’s a way to identify a substance regardless of sample size.
Significant figures communicate precision:

All non-zero digits count.
Zeros between other digits count (102 has 3 sig figs).
Leading zeros never count (0.0025 has 2 sig figs).
Trailing zeros count only if there’s a decimal point (100. has 3 sig figs; 100 has 1).








TipQuick trick



When multiplying/dividing, your answer can only have as many sig figs as your least precise measurement. When adding/subtracting, match the fewest decimal places.

title: Unit 1: Matter & Measurement
text:
Practice Problems

Classify each as an element, compound, homogeneous mixture, or heterogeneous mixture: (a) air, (b) table salt (NaCl), (c) trail mix, (d) copper wire.







NoteSolution






Air — homogeneous mixture (mostly N₂ and O₂ blended uniformly)
NaCl — compound (fixed ratio of Na and Cl)
Trail mix — heterogeneous mixture (you can see distinct pieces)
Copper wire — element





A piece of metal has a mass of 47.5 g and a volume of 6.2 cm³. What is its density, with the correct number of sig figs?







NoteSolution





Density = 47.5 g ÷ 6.2 cm³ = 7.66… g/cm³
The least precise measurement (6.2) has 2 sig figs, so round to 7.7 g/cm³.




How many significant figures are in each: (a) 0.00420, (b) 3,050, (c) 3,050., (d) 12.300?







NoteSolution






3 sig figs — leading zeros don’t count, trailing zero after the 2 does
3 sig figs — trailing zero with no decimal doesn’t count
4 sig figs — the decimal point makes the trailing zero count
5 sig figs — all digits count once a decimal point is present

title: Unit 2: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table
text:
An atom has three particles:



Particle
Charge
Location
Mass




Proton
+1
Nucleus
~1 amu


Neutron
0
Nucleus
~1 amu


Electron
-1
Electron cloud
~0 (negligible)




Atomic number (Z) = number of protons — this defines the element.
Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons (same Z, different A). Written as, e.g., carbon-14.
In a neutral atom, electrons = protons. Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons.




Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number into rows (periods) and columns (groups/families). Elements in the same group share similar chemical behavior because they have the same number of valence electrons (outermost shell).
Key periodic trends, and why they happen:

Atomic radius decreases left→right (more protons pull electrons in tighter), increases top→bottom (more electron shells).
Ionization energy (energy to remove an electron) increases left→right, decreases top→bottom — it’s the opposite pattern from radius, because atoms held tightly are harder to strip an electron from.
Electronegativity (how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons) follows the same trend as ionization energy, peaking at fluorine.







TipMemory anchor



Think of it as a “diagonal pull toward the top-right corner”: radius shrinks and pulling power grows as you move toward fluorine/helium, because the nucleus has more protons but electrons stay in a shell close to it.

title: Unit 2: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table
text:
Practice Problems

An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons, and 17 electrons. Identify the element, write the mass number, and state whether it’s a neutral atom or an ion.







NoteSolution





17 protons → atomic number 17 → chlorine (Cl). Mass number = 17 protons + 18 neutrons = 35. Protons (17) = electrons (17) → neutral atom (this is Cl-35).




Without looking at a periodic table, predict which has the larger atomic radius: sodium (Na) or chlorine (Cl). Explain why.







NoteSolution





Sodium is larger. Both are in period 3, but chlorine has more protons pulling its electron cloud inward, while sodium’s weaker nuclear pull lets its outer electron sit farther out.




Rank these by increasing ionization energy: potassium (K), lithium (Li), fluorine (F).







NoteSolution





K < Li < F. Ionization energy decreases down a group (K is below Li) and increases across a period toward the right (F is far right, hardest to strip an electron from).

title: Unit 3: Chemical Bonding
text:
Atoms bond to become more stable, generally by achieving a full outer shell (the octet rule — 8 valence electrons, like the noble gases).


Form between a metal and a nonmetal. The metal loses electrons (becomes a positive cation), and the nonmetal gains them (becomes a negative anion). The opposite charges attract.

Example: Na loses 1 electron → Na⁺; Cl gains 1 electron → Cl⁻ → NaCl
Naming: metal name + nonmetal root + “-ide” (sodium chloride)




Form between two nonmetals, which share electrons instead of transferring them.

Nonpolar covalent: electrons shared roughly equally (same or very similar elements, e.g., O₂)
Polar covalent: shared unequally because one atom is more electronegative (e.g., H₂O — oxygen pulls harder)
Naming: use prefixes (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-…) for each element, e.g., CO₂ = carbon dioxide





Count total valence electrons (add up group numbers).
Place least electronegative atom in the center (never H or F).
Connect atoms with single bonds (2 electrons each).
Fill remaining electrons as lone pairs to satisfy octets, outer atoms first.
If the center atom is short of an octet, turn a lone pair into a double/triple bond.







TipTelling ionic and covalent apart fast



Metal + nonmetal → ionic. Nonmetal + nonmetal → covalent. Check a periodic table: metals are the majority on the left/middle, nonmetals are on the upper right (plus hydrogen).

text:
Practice Problems

Predict whether each compound is ionic or covalent: (a) MgO, (b) CO₂, (c) KBr, (d) NH₃.







NoteSolution






MgO — ionic (metal Mg + nonmetal O)
CO₂ — covalent (both nonmetals)
KBr — ionic (metal K + nonmetal Br)
NH₃ — covalent (both nonmetals)





Name the ionic compound formed between calcium and fluorine, and write its formula.







NoteSolution





Calcium forms Ca²⁺, fluorine forms F⁻. You need 2 fluorines to balance the +2 charge: CaF₂, named calcium fluoride.




Draw the Lewis structure for CO₂ (carbon center) and state how many bonding pairs surround the carbon.







NoteSolution





Total valence electrons: C (4) + 2×O (6 each) = 16. Carbon in the center, single-bonded to each oxygen uses 4 electrons, leaving 12 for lone pairs. Giving each oxygen 3 lone pairs only satisfies their octet, but carbon has just 4 electrons around it (needs 8) — so each C–O bond becomes a double bond (O=C=O). Carbon ends up with 2 double bonds (4 bonding pairs total), each oxygen keeps 2 lone pairs.

title: Unit 1: Thinking Geographically
text:
Absolute location: an exact position (coordinates, address).
Relative location: where something is in relation to other things (“east of the river”).
Spatial distribution: how something is arranged across an area — described by:

Density (how much/many per unit area)
Concentration (clustered vs. dispersed)
Pattern (geometric, random, linear…)





In geography, scale means the level of analysis — local, regional, national, or global. The “scale of analysis” matters: a trend that appears at the national level (e.g., “the US is aging”) can look totally different city by city. This is related to the modifiable areal unit problem — how you draw boundaries on a map can change what pattern you appear to see.




Formal region: shares an official/measurable trait (a country, a climate zone)
Functional region: organized around a hub/node (a pizza delivery zone, a metro transit system)
Perceptual (vernacular) region: defined by people’s mental image, not hard data (“the South,” “the Midwest”)




Geographers study how humans adapt to, modify, and depend on their environment (e.g., building levees, irrigation, urban heat islands).






TipExam-writing tip



When APHG asks you to “explain” a spatial pattern, always connect it to a process — don’t just describe the map, say why it looks that way (migration, trade routes, physical geography, policy, etc.).

title: Unit 1: Thinking Geographically
text:
Practice Problems

Classify each region type: (a) the Sun Belt, (b) the state of Ohio, (c) the coverage area of a local pizza delivery chain.







NoteSolution






Sun Belt — perceptual/vernacular region (no official boundary, based on shared perception)
Ohio — formal region (official political boundary)
Pizza delivery zone — functional region (organized around a central node, the store)





A news report says “crime is rising in the Midwest.” Explain one problem with analyzing this claim only at that scale.







NoteSolution





The Midwest is a huge, varied area — a regional-scale rise could be driven by one or two cities while most places see no change, or the pattern could reverse itself at the city or neighborhood scale. Zooming to a finer scale of analysis is necessary before drawing conclusions about causes.




Is “distance from the coast” an example of absolute or relative location? Explain.







NoteSolution





Relative location — it describes position in relation to another feature (the coast), not a fixed coordinate.

title: AP Human Geography
text:
AP Human Geography (APHG) studies patterns and processes of how humans organize themselves across space — where people live, how culture spreads, and how political boundaries form. It’s less about memorizing maps and more about explaining why patterns look the way they do.

Units

Thinking Geographically — maps, spatial concepts, scale, and geographic reasoning
Population & Migration — population growth, the demographic transition, push/pull factors
Culture — cultural landscapes, diffusion, language and religion patterns







Note



Later units (political geography, agriculture, urbanization, industry/development) follow the same page pattern.

title: Unit 3: Grammar & Mechanics
text:
Independent clause: has a subject and verb, can stand alone as a sentence.
Dependent (subordinate) clause: has a subject and verb, but cannot stand alone (starts with words like because, although, when, which).

Common errors come from mishandling these:

Run-on sentence: two independent clauses jammed together with no punctuation/connector.
Comma splice: two independent clauses joined with just a comma (needs a conjunction, semicolon, or period instead).
Sentence fragment: a dependent clause (or incomplete thought) punctuated as if it were a full sentence.





Semicolon: joins two related independent clauses without a conjunction (“The exam was hard; everyone left exhausted.”)
Comma before a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) when joining two independent clauses: “She studied all night, but the test was still tough.”
No comma needed if the conjunction joins just a verb phrase, not a full second clause: “She studied all night and passed the test.” (no comma — “passed the test” isn’t a full independent clause with its own subject)
Apostrophes: show possession (the dog’s leash) or contraction (it’s = it is) — never just to make a word plural.





its (possessive) vs. it’s (it is)
their (possessive) vs. there (place) vs. they’re (they are)
your (possessive) vs. you’re (you are)
affect (usually a verb, to influence) vs. effect (usually a noun, a result)







TipQuick fragment test



Read the clause alone. If it starts with a word like because, although, since, when, while, which and doesn’t have another independent clause attached, it’s a fragment — it’s answering a question (“why?” “when?”) that was never asked.

title: Unit 3: Grammar & Mechanics
text:
Practice Problems

Identify the error and fix it: “I finished my homework, I went outside to play.”







NoteSolution





This is a comma splice (two independent clauses joined by only a comma). Fix options: “I finished my homework, so I went outside to play.” or “I finished my homework; I went outside to play.” or “I finished my homework. I went outside to play.”




Is this a complete sentence or a fragment? “Because the weather turned cold overnight.”







NoteSolution





Fragment — it’s a dependent clause with no independent clause attached. It needs something like: “Because the weather turned cold overnight, we brought the plants inside.”




Choose the correct word: “___ going to need ___ umbrella because ___ raining outside.” (they’re/their/there, its/it’s, its/it’s)







NoteSolution





“They’re going to need their umbrella because it’s raining outside.” (They’re = they are; their = possessive; it’s = it is)

title: Unit 1: Close Reading & Literary Analysis
text:
A topic is what a work is about in one or two words (loss, ambition, family). A theme is the insight or claim the work makes about that topic — a full sentence. “Ambition” is a topic; “unchecked ambition corrodes relationships” is a theme.




Tone = the author’s/narrator’s attitude toward the subject (sarcastic, reverent, bitter).
Mood = the emotional atmosphere the reader feels (tense, nostalgic, eerie).

These are shaped by diction (word choice), syntax (sentence structure), and imagery.










Device
What it does




Symbolism
An object/image represents a larger idea


Foreshadowing
Hints at events to come


Irony
Gap between expectation and reality (situational, verbal, dramatic)


Motif
A recurring element that reinforces a theme


Characterization
How a character is revealed (direct statement vs. actions/dialogue = indirect)






The core move is: claim → evidence → analysis. Don’t just quote the text — explain how the quote’s specific word choice or structure supports your claim. A weak analysis restates the quote; a strong one explains the effect of the technique.






TipUpgrade weak analysis



Instead of “This shows the author uses imagery,” try: “The imagery of ‘rust creeping along the fence’ mirrors the slow decay of the family’s relationship, making the abstract idea of estrangement feel physically inevitable.”

title: Unit 1: Close Reading & Literary Analysis
text:
Practice Problems

Turn this topic into a theme statement: “isolation” (as explored in a story where a character withdraws after a loss).







NoteSolution





Sample theme: “Isolation, while initially protective, ultimately prevents healing by cutting a person off from the support they need.” (Any full-sentence claim that goes beyond the single word works.)




A character is described by the narrator as “honest and kind,” but the story shows them lying to protect their own reputation. What’s the difference between the direct and indirect characterization here, and what might it suggest?







NoteSolution





The narrator’s description is direct characterization (“honest and kind” stated outright). The character’s actions (lying) are indirect characterization. The contradiction suggests unreliable narration or that the character’s self-image doesn’t match reality — a gap worth analyzing.




Identify the device: a storm builds throughout a chapter, then breaks into violence right as two characters have their final argument.







NoteSolution





This is symbolism (the storm represents the emotional conflict) and could also be discussed as foreshadowing if earlier hints pointed to the coming argument.

title: Unit 3: Congruence & Similarity
text:
Two triangles are congruent (identical in shape and size) if you can show one of these matches, without needing to check all 6 parts:

SSS: all three sides match
SAS: two sides and the included angle (the angle between them) match
ASA: two angles and the included side match
AAS: two angles and a non-included side match
HL (right triangles only): hypotenuse and one leg match







TipWatch out for “SSA”



There’s no such thing as an “SSA” shortcut — two sides and a non-included angle do not guarantee congruence (it can produce two different triangles). Always double check the angle is between the two given sides for SAS.





Two triangles are similar (same shape, proportional size) if their corresponding angles are congruent and their corresponding sides are in the same ratio. Shortcuts:

AA (Angle-Angle): if two angles match, the third automatically matches too (angles sum to 180°), so the triangles are similar.
SAS similarity: two sides in the same ratio, and the included angle congruent.
SSS similarity: all three sides in the same ratio.





Pythagorean Theorem: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle).
Special right triangles: 45-45-90 triangles have legs in ratio 1:1:√2; 30-60-90 triangles have sides in ratio 1:√3:2.

title: Unit 3: Congruence & Similarity
text:
Practice Problems

Two triangles share two pairs of congruent angles: 50° and 70°. Are they similar? Why?







NoteSolution





Yes — similar by AA. If two angles match, the third must also match (since angles sum to 180° in every triangle), so the shapes are guaranteed similar.




A right triangle has legs of 6 and 8. Find the hypotenuse.







NoteSolution





6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100. √100 = 10




Triangle ABC has sides 4, 6, 8. Triangle DEF has sides 6, 9, 12. Are they similar? What’s the scale factor?







NoteSolution





Check the ratios: 6/4 = 1.5, 9/6 = 1.5, 12/8 = 1.5 — all equal, so yes, similar by SSS similarity, with a scale factor of 1.5.

title: Unit 1: Foundations & Proof Basics
text:
Point: a location, no size (labeled with a capital letter)
Line: extends infinitely in both directions, no thickness
Plane: a flat surface extending infinitely in all directions

From these, we define segments (part of a line with two endpoints) and rays (starts at a point, extends infinitely one direction).




Complementary angles: sum to 90°
Supplementary angles: sum to 180°
Vertical angles: opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines — always congruent
Linear pair: two adjacent angles that form a straight line — always supplementary




A postulate (or axiom) is accepted as true without proof (e.g., “through any two points there is exactly one line”). A theorem is a statement proven using postulates, definitions, and previously proven theorems.



A proof is a logical argument that gets from given information to a conclusion, one justified step at a time.



Statement
Reason




∠1 and ∠2 form a linear pair
Given


∠1 + ∠2 = 180°
Definition of linear pair


∠1 = 70°
Given


∠2 = 110°
Substitution / Subtraction property









TipHow to start any proof



Write down exactly what’s “Given” as your first line, and what you need to prove as your last line. Then work backward from the conclusion, asking “what would let me claim this?” — that usually reveals the missing middle steps.

title: Unit 1: Foundations & Proof Basics
text:
Practice Problems

Two angles are supplementary. One measures 112°. Find the other.







NoteSolution





180° − 112° = 68°




Two lines intersect, forming four angles. One angle measures 55°. Find the measures of the other three.







NoteSolution





The angle vertical to the 55° angle is also 55° (vertical angles are congruent). The two angles adjacent to it form linear pairs with it: 180° − 55° = 125° each.




Fill in the missing reason: Given ∠A ≅ ∠B and ∠B ≅ ∠C, prove ∠A ≅ ∠C. The reason is ______.







NoteSolution





Transitive property of congruence — if two things are each congruent to a third thing, they’re congruent to each other.
